questions.q: According to this lesson, what does "assume breach" mean as a design constraint?
options: A policy statement that security awareness training has been completed
A promise that breaches will never happen if enough tools are purchased
Building a system as if an attacker already holds a working foothold inside it right now, not as a future possibility
A compliance checkbox required for a SOC 2 audit
questions.explain: Assume breach reframes the design question from "how do we keep the attacker out" to "given the attacker is already in, what can they reach and how fast do we notice."

questions.q: What is the "slogan problem" this lesson describes?
options: Organizations that use the phrase "assume breach" without changing the underlying architecture — flat networks, shared admin credentials, no logging on critical segments
A naming convention issue where different teams use different terms for the same control
The fact that marketing teams overuse the term Zero Trust in advertising
A legal requirement to disclose breach assumptions in public filings
questions.explain: The slogan problem is teams adopting the phrase as a value statement while the actual architecture still has flat trust zones, standing admin access, and no meaningful containment design.

questions.q: Which of the following is a genuine containment question, as distinguished from a prevention question in this lesson?
options: Is this credential protected with a strong password policy?
Does this workload have antivirus installed?
Is MFA enabled for this account?
If this specific credential is phished right now, what can the attacker reach with it?
questions.explain: Prevention questions ask whether protection is in place; the containment question assumes protection already failed and asks what is in scope as a result.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that assume breach ties together the identity and segmentation work from earlier chapters?
options: Because identity and segmentation are unrelated to containment and are covered only for completeness
Because least-privilege access and micro-segmentation exist specifically to limit what a compromised foothold can do, which is the containment goal assume breach names
Because continuous access evaluation replaces the need for segmentation entirely
Because Zero Trust requires removing all network boundaries, making segmentation obsolete
questions.explain: Just-enough-access and micro-segmentation were built in earlier chapters precisely to limit what a single compromised credential or device can reach — the same goal assume breach makes explicit.

questions.q: What artifact-based test does this lesson propose for whether a team genuinely assumes breach, versus treating it as a slogan?
options: Whether the security team has a dedicated budget line for Zero Trust
Whether every employee has signed an acceptable-use policy
Whether a documented blast-radius estimate, a lateral-movement analysis, and a containment plan can actually be produced in a design review
Whether the organization has purchased a SOAR platform
questions.explain: The lesson proposes that assume breach is only meaningful if a design review can produce specific, checkable artifacts — a blast-radius estimate, a lateral-movement analysis, and a containment plan — not just a stated value.
